Claudius
KLAW-dee-us
n. (proper, a Roman emperor; also a chief captain in Jerusalem)
Latin Claudius, a Roman family name. The Authorized Version uses it of two men: Claudius Caesar, the fourth emperor, and Claudius Lysias, the chief captain whose letter sent Paul to Caesarea.

Biblical Definition

Agabus came down to Antioch and “signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar” (Acts 11:28) — and the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief to the brethren in Judaea. The emperor appears again as the cause of a providential meeting: at Corinth Paul “found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:)” (Acts 18:2). An imperial expulsion order put the apostle in a tentmaker's house. The second Claudius is the officer who rescued Paul from the mob and later from an ambush, and whose letter is quoted verbatim: “Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting” (Acts 23:26). Roman law, Roman roads and Roman edicts all serve the spread of the gospel in Acts without intending to.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of the Roman emperor in whose days the great dearth came, and of the chief captain Claudius Lysias.

expand to see more

CAESAR, n. A title of the Roman emperors, derived from the family name of Julius Caesar.

DEARTH, n. Scarcity; such a want of any thing as renders it dear; particularly, a scarcity of food.

EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince.

CHIEF CAPTAIN, n. In the New Testament, the tribune commanding a Roman cohort, as Claudius Lysias at Jerusalem.

CITIZENSHIP, n. The state of being vested with the rights and privileges of a citizen.

Key Scripture

Acts 11:28 — "And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar."

Acts 18:2 — "And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them."

Acts 23:26 — "Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting."

Acts 11:29 — "Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea:"

Modern Corruption

The state is treated either as the church's enemy to be defied or as her patron to be courted; Acts shows an emperor's expulsion order and a tribune's letter serving the gospel without either man intending it.

expand to see more

Two settled attitudes toward civil power crowd out the biblical one. The first treats the magistrate as simply hostile, so that every edict is persecution and every officer an enemy. The second courts the state for favour and shapes the church's message to keep it. Acts 18:2 will not fit either. Claudius commanded all Jews to depart from Rome — an unjust order that uprooted households — and the immediate result in the text is that Paul found Aquila and Priscilla, worked at tents with them, and gained two of the most useful colleagues in the New Testament. God's providence is not obstructed by an unjust decree; it runs through it.

Claudius Lysias fills out the picture from the other side. He bound Paul to examine him by scourging, released him when he learned he was a Roman, rescued him from forty men under an oath to kill him, and wrote a self-serving letter that quietly improved his own conduct in the telling. Paul used the protection, appealed to his citizenship, and was carried to Rome by the very system that had chained him. The believer's duty is to honour the magistrate, to use lawful protection without shame, and to obey God rather than men where the two conflict — and to expect God to reach his ends through officials who are serving their own.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Klaudios (G2804), Claudius; limos (G3042), a famine or dearth; chiliarchos (G5506), a chief captain; diatasso (G1299), to command or ordain.

expand to see more

Greek Klaudios (G2804) — Claudius; used of the emperor and of Claudius Lysias.

Greek limos (G3042) — famine, dearth; the scarcity Agabus foretold by the Spirit.

Greek chiliarchos (G5506) — a commander of a thousand, a chief captain; Lysias's rank.

Greek diatasso (G1299) — to arrange, to command; Claudius commanded the Jews to depart.

Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministry, relief; what the disciples sent to Judaea in the dearth.

Usage

"“Which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar” — a prophecy dated."

"“Because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome”."

"“Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting”."
